title: Sonnet 29 – ‘I think of thee!’
published: published 1850, in Sonnets from the Portuguese

facts.type: Petrarchan sonnet (14 lines, rhyme ABBAABBA CDCDCD)
facts.exam: Yes: printed in June 2022 (on the separate Covid-era poetry paper, “ideas about the power of love”); also a suggested partner in the 2018, 2019, Nov 2021 and 2024 mark schemes
facts.partner: Porphyria’s Lover (your anchor); Love’s Philosophy also works well

cards.story: A woman thinks about the man she loves while he is away. Her thoughts grow round him like wild vines round a tree, until she can hardly see him. She orders him to come back and shake them off.
cards.message: Love is so powerful it can take over your whole mind. But thinking about someone is no substitute for being with them: the real person is better than any daydream.
cards.why: Barrett Browning wrote the poem in secret while Robert Browning was courting her (1845–46). It is one of 44 love sonnets published in 1850 as Sonnets from the Portuguese. Britannica; poets.org; Victorian Web

title_note.heading: The title
title_note.text: “Sonnet 29” means it is the 29th poem in a sequence of 44 love sonnets. In the original book it has only a number (XXIX); the anthology adds the first words, “I think of thee!”, as a subtitle. anthology point: our reading Watch how the last line answers the title: “I do not think of thee”. The poem travels from thinking about him to being with him. Beware: the sonnets were written in English, not Portuguese. The title Sonnets from the Portuguese was “a ruse to disguise the sonnets' personal nature”; it played on Robert’s pet name for her, “the Portuguese”.

synopsis.setup: The speaker talks directly to the man she loves (<q>“thee”</q>). He is not with her, so all she has are her thoughts about him.

steps.text: Her thoughts <q>“twine and bud”</q> round him, <q>“as wild vines, about a tree”</q>. They put out broad leaves until all you can see is <q>“the straggling green which hides the wood”</q>. Her thoughts now hide the real man.
The turn: <q>“Yet, O my palm-tree”</q>. She will not accept <q>“my thoughts instead of thee”</q>, because he is <q>“dearer, better!”</q> than anything she imagines.

She orders him to come back at once (<q>“instantly / Renew thy presence”</q>). Like a strong tree, he should shake his branches and strip his trunk bare, so the vines of her thoughts <q>“Drop heavily down, – burst, shattered, everywhere!”</q>
When he is there, she feels <q>“deep joy”</q> just to see and hear him and to <q>“breathe within thy shadow a new air”</q>. Then she does not need to think of him: <q>“I am too near thee.”</q>

synopsis.turn: The turning point (line 5): “Yet, O my palm-tree, be it understood”. Sonnets usually turn at line 9, but this one turns at line 5, as soon as she realises her thoughts are smothering him. AQA’s examiners report that many students wrote about “the unusual placing of the volta”.
synopsis.ending: The last line repeats the first, but in the negative: <q>“I think of thee!”</q> becomes <q>“I do not think of thee”</q>. Examiners report “some difference of opinion”. Some students saw that the real man’s presence is better than “any amount of reflection, dwelling or fantasising about him”. Others argued she has “gone off” him, or finds reality poorer than the fantasy. You can mention both.
synopsis.tone: Excited, passionate and commanding. It is full of exclamation marks and orders (<q>“Renew”</q>, <q>“Rustle”</q>), and it ends in calm, happy closeness.

poem_intro: Highlighted words are the ones worth quoting in the exam. The poem is one 14-line block; the notes follow its sense units.

poem_blocks.text:
I think of thee! – my thoughts do twine and bud
About thee, as wild vines, about a tree,
Put out broad leaves, and soon there’s nought to see
Except the straggling green which hides the wood.
poem_blocks.note: The opening exclamation shows how excited she is. Her thoughts are like wild vines: they “twine” (wind round) and “bud” (grow) round him, the tree. Soon there is nothing to see but the messy (“straggling”) leaves, which hide the “wood” (the tree trunk). Her thoughts are growing so fast that they hide the real man. Love is powerful, but it could smother him.

poem_blocks.text:
Yet, O my palm-tree, be it understood
I will not have my thoughts instead of thee
Who art dearer, better! Rather, instantly
poem_blocks.note: “Yet” marks the turn. She now calls him “my palm-tree”: a tall, proud, exotic tree, and “my” shows he belongs to her heart. She makes a firm statement: she will not settle for thoughts “instead of” him, because the real man is “dearer, better!”

poem_blocks.text:
Renew thy presence; as a strong tree should,
Rustle thy boughs and set thy trunk all bare,
And let these bands of greenery which insphere thee
Drop heavily down, – burst, shattered, everywhere!
poem_blocks.note: A string of orders: come back (“Renew thy presence”), shake your branches (“boughs”), strip your trunk bare. The vines are now “bands”, like ropes, that “insphere” (wrap all round) him. She wants them to fall and break apart. The violent verbs “burst, shattered” show her thoughts being destroyed so the real man can be free.

poem_blocks.text:
Because, in this deep joy to see and hear thee
And breathe within thy shadow a new air,
I do not think of thee – I am too near thee.
poem_blocks.note: “Because” gives her reason. When he is with her, she uses her senses (see, hear, breathe), not just her mind. Standing in his “shadow” she breathes “a new air”: love gives her fresh life. The last line answers the first: she no longer needs to think of him, because she is “too near”.

quotes.q: my thoughts do twine and bud
quotes.means: my thoughts wind round you and keep growing.
quotes.why: starts the extended metaphor: love is alive and growing, but also clinging.

quotes.q: as wild vines, about a tree,
quotes.means: like wild climbing plants wrapped round a tree.
quotes.why: “wild” suggests her love is out of control; vines can strangle the tree they climb. AQA’s examiners saw students link it to her “obsession” and “suffocating passion”.

quotes.q: the straggling green which hides the wood.
quotes.means: the messy leaves that hide the tree trunk.
quotes.why: her thoughts about him now hide the real man: the power of love to cloud your judgement.

quotes.q: Yet, O my palm-tree, be it understood
quotes.means: But, my darling, let me make this clear.
quotes.why: the turn (volta) comes early, at line 5. “O” is a passionate cry, and “my” shows how much he means to her.

quotes.q: I will not have my thoughts instead of thee
quotes.means: I refuse to have only thoughts in place of you.
quotes.why: a firm, decisive statement: she wants the real person, not a fantasy. The woman takes charge.

quotes.q: Drop heavily down, – burst, shattered, everywhere!
quotes.means: let my thoughts fall off and break apart.
quotes.why: violent, explosive verbs: love is so strong it destroys what came before. The dash and exclamation make it sound sudden.
quotes.tech: list of three; violent verbs; exclamation

quotes.q: I do not think of thee – I am too near thee.
quotes.means: I don’t need to think about you, because I’m right beside you.
quotes.why: turns the opening line round. Some students read it as joy at being together; others read it as disappointment. AQA’s examiners recorded both readings.

form.heading: The form: a Petrarchan sonnet with an early turn
explain: A sonnet is a 14-line poem, usually in iambic pentameter (ten syllables, five beats per line). Britannica; poets.org; Poetry Archive
The Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet has an octave (8 lines) rhyming ABBAABBA and a sestet (6 lines). The octave sets up a problem; the sestet answers it. Britannica; Poetry Archive; poets.org
The volta (turn) is a shift in thought, “often indicated by such initial words as But, Yet, or And yet”. It usually comes between lines 8 and 9. Britannica; poets.org

Traditionally a man wrote the sonnets to an idealised woman: Petrarch wrote “317 sonnets, addressed to his idealized beloved, Laura”. Barrett Browning’s sequence revived the love sonnet in the 19th century. Britannica
this_poem: Strict rhyme: the octave rhymes ABBAABBA (bud, tree, see, wood …) and the sestet CDCDCD (bare, thee, everywhere …). It follows the Petrarchan pattern exactly. our count from the anthology

An early turn: the volta comes at line 5, with “Yet”, not at line 9. The vines take only four lines to grow too thick; she reacts at once. our reading; many students wrote about “the unusual placing of the volta” (AQA June 2022 examiners' report)
Spilling over: from “Rather” in line 7, one long sentence runs across the octave–sestet break to line 11. Her feelings will not stay inside the form’s neat boxes. our reading

A woman in charge: here the woman is the lover and speaker, and the man is the beloved (the tree). A student essay on the Victorian Web, quoting a critic, says writing love sonnets “from the female perspective” was seen as “not the sphere of a Victorian woman”. Victorian Web one source; link to this poem is our reading
The ending circles back: three of the sestet’s six lines end on “thee” (“insphere thee”, “hear thee”, “near thee”). The poem keeps landing on him, just as her mind does. our reading

Keep form linked to meaning: after comments on “the ABBA rhyme scheme”, examiners warn that comments on poetic construction can become “rather descriptive” and interrupt “a student’s focus on examining words, ideas and meanings”. AQA June 2022 examiners' report
form.say: A sentence you could use: Barrett Browning uses the traditional love sonnet but turns it early, at line 5 with “Yet”, as if the power of her love is too urgent to wait for line 9; the woman, not the man, is the one who speaks and commands.

methods.title: The vine and the tree
methods.text: The whole octave is one picture: her thoughts are <q>“wild vines”</q> and he is the tree. It shows love as alive and growing, but also clinging and smothering. Most students in 2022 wrote about this image.
methods.def: a comparison that is kept going over several lines or a whole poem.

methods.title: Exclamations
methods.text: <q>“I think of thee!”</q>, <q>“dearer, better!”</q>, <q>“shattered, everywhere!”</q> The exclamation marks show how excited and overwhelmed she is. AQA’s mark scheme points to the “exclamatory language” of this poem.
methods.def: sentences ending in “!” that show strong feeling.

methods.title: Giving orders
methods.text: <q>“Renew thy presence”</q>, <q>“Rustle thy boughs”</q>, <q>“set thy trunk all bare”</q>. A woman commanding a man was unusual for the time. Love gives her power and confidence.
methods.def: command verbs that tell someone what to do.

methods.title: Thee, thee, thee
methods.text: She addresses him directly all the way through. <q>“thee”</q> comes in the first line’s exclamation and is the poem’s very last word; three lines of the sestet end on it. He is at the centre of everything she says, which shows how love fills her whole mind.
methods.def: speaking straight to someone, using “you” (here the old form “thee”).

warn: Examiners warn: “AO3 is much more appropriately addressed by focusing on ideas such as the power of love to make someone obsessive, very unhappy, grief-stricken, unbalanced, etc than writing about, for example, Browning’s father’s attitude, the sonnet written in Portuguese or Browning’s illness.” They also warn that comments on “the ABBA rhyme scheme” can become “rather descriptive”. AQA June 2022 examiners' report

timeline.text: Elizabeth Barrett born in County Durham, the eldest of twelve children
Falls seriously ill at about 15; her health is permanently affected
Her Poems are “enthusiastically received”: she is already a famous poet
Robert Browning writes: “I love your verses with all my heart” … “and I love you too”
Over 570 love letters, almost daily; she secretly begins the sonnets
Secret wedding in London; a week later they leave for Italy
Sonnets from the Portuguese published, including Sonnet 29

items.text: Born in 1806 in County Durham, she was a famous poet before she met Robert Browning: her 1844 Poems were “enthusiastically received”.
She wrote against injustice, including slavery (“The Runaway Slave at Pilgrim's Point”), and supported Italian freedom.
Her verse novel Aurora Leigh is “now considered an early feminist text”.
She was often ill and lived quietly in her strict father’s London house. Background only: AQA says her illness and her father are not good AO3 points on their own.
items.src: Britannica; poets.org; AQA June 2022 examiners' report

items.text: In January 1845 the poet Robert Browning, a stranger, wrote to her: “I love your verses with all my heart, dear Miss Barrett” and ended “and I love you too.” They met that summer.
items.use: the power of love · romantic love

items.text: They wrote to each other “almost daily” from January 1845 to September 1846: over 570 letters.
The courtship “was kept a close secret”. They married secretly on 12 September 1846 and left for Italy a week later.
Much of the courtship happened in letters and short visits, so she spent a lot of time thinking about him rather than with him. That is exactly the gap the poem explores.
The sonnets were “written in secret before her marriage”. She began them in 1845, the year the courtship started.
She did not show them to Robert until after they were married (in 1847, says Britannica).
They were published in 1850 as Sonnets from the Portuguese, 44 sonnets in all. The title was “a ruse” to hide how personal they were, playing on Robert’s pet name for her.
The sequence is “one of the most widely known collections of love lyrics in English”. Sonnet 43 begins “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.”
items.use: the sonnet as a love poem

cards.title: What examiners say (use this for AO3)

items.text: Students wrote about “the extended metaphor of the vines” and linked it to “the speaker’s obsession with and suffocating passion for her lover”.
The mark scheme suggests writing about the power of love “as overwhelming, or transformative, or invoking of happiness”, and “the use of nature as image in poetry”.
AQA links this poem with “joy” and “more positive views of love”, and with “hope/lasting nature of romantic relationships”.
AO3 works best through ideas: “the power of love to make someone obsessive, very unhappy, grief-stricken, unbalanced, etc”. Love that affects “your whole being” is “a universal thing”.

context.ao3: Putting it into an answer (AO3): keep context tied to ideas. Barrett Browning wrote as a woman in a form traditionally used by men to praise women, so here the woman is the one who desires, speaks and gives orders. Link this to the power of love: it can take over your whole mind (the vines), but it can also make you bold and joyful when you are finally together.

comparisons.aqa: AQA: the 2022 mark scheme (Sonnet 29 question) names Porphyria’s Lover under “the negative powerful effects of love”; the 2022 report says it “worked well”; both are suggested in 2018 and 2024
similar: Both speakers are obsessed with the person they love: <q>“my thoughts do twine and bud”</q> and <q>“Porphyria worshipped me”</q>.
Both use plant images for love: her thoughts are <q>“wild vines”</q>; he opens Porphyria’s dead eyelids <q>“As a shut bud that holds a bee,”</q>.
Both are told in the first person, so we only hear one side of the relationship.
different: Positive or negative: Barrett Browning shows love’s joyful power; Browning shows its destructive power.
What they want: she wants her living lover beside her: “Renew thy presence;”. He wants to freeze one moment: “That moment she was mine, mine, fair,”, so he kills her.
Freedom or possession: she lets her clinging thoughts “burst, shattered, everywhere!” to set him free; he traps Porphyria for ever: “And all night long we have not stirred,”.
Closeness: her ending, “I am too near thee.”, is two living people together; his is a man beside a corpse.

comparisons.aqa: AQA: 2022 mark scheme (Sonnet 29 question) names Love’s Philosophy for “imagery used to present ideas about the power of love”; Nov 2021 mark scheme names both for “positive effects of strong feelings”; 2022 report: “worked well”
similar: Both use nature to show love wrapping two people together: <q>“In one another's being mingle”</q> and <q>“as wild vines, about a tree,”</q>.
Both speakers want the loved one’s physical presence, not just thoughts or words: <q>“If thou kiss not me?”</q> and <q>“Renew thy presence;”</q>.
different: Who speaks: a man trying to persuade a woman, against a woman longing for a man who is away.
Ending: Shelley ends on an unanswered question; Barrett Browning ends together and joyful: “I am too near thee.”
Tone: Shelley pleads and argues; Barrett Browning commands (“Rustle thy boughs”).
Form: two neat 8-line stanzas against a 14-line sonnet, the traditional form for love poetry.

comparisons.aqa: AQA: 2022 mark scheme (Sonnet 29 question) names Neutral Tones under “the negative powerful effects of love”; 2022 report: “worked well”
similar: Both use a tree and plants to show love: Barrett Browning’s vines and <q>“palm-tree”</q>; Hardy’s leaves <q>“fallen from an ash, and were grey.”</q>
Both speakers talk straight to the lover (<q>“thee”</q>, <q>“Your eyes on me”</q>) and both are shaped by love’s power over the mind.
different: Living or dead: her nature is growing (“twine and bud”); his is dying (“the starving sod”).
Lesson learned: she learns the real man is “dearer, better!” than her thoughts; he learns “keen lessons that love deceives,”.
Ending: her poem ends in closeness and “deep joy”; his ends with a memory of loss that returns to the pond where it began.

exam_box.question: A likely question: Compare how poets present ideas about the power of love in ‘Sonnet 29’ and in one other poem from ‘Love and relationships’. (AQA asked exactly this in June 2022.)
exam_box.thesis: Both Barrett Browning and Browning show love as a force strong enough to take over a person’s mind, but while Barrett Browning’s speaker breaks free of her obsession to enjoy her lover’s real presence, Browning’s speaker turns obsession into possession and destroys the woman he loves.
exam_box.para: Both poets show love as obsessive. Barrett Browning’s thoughts <q>“twine and bud”</q> round her lover <q>“as wild vines, about a tree,”</q>, suggesting a passion that grows until it hides <q>“the wood”</q>. Similarly, Browning’s speaker is consumed by the thought that <q>“Porphyria worshipped me”</q>. However, the two speakers respond in opposite ways. Barrett Browning orders her thoughts to <q>“burst, shattered, everywhere!”</q>: the violent verbs destroy her fantasy so that the real man can be free, and the poem ends in <q>“deep joy”</q>. Browning’s speaker instead wants to freeze a fantasy for ever: <q>“That moment she was mine, mine, fair”</q>. The repeated possessive shows love becoming ownership. Perhaps Barrett Browning suggests love is powerful enough to transform us, while Browning warns it can become dangerous when it turns into control.
why: Thesis answers the question (the power of love) in one sentence and names both poems’ ideas
Short quotations from both poems, with methods named (extended metaphor, violent verbs, repeated possessive)
Compares throughout (“Similarly”, “However”, “instead”) and ends with a tentative judgement (“Perhaps”)
